newsitem.title: USA: Giuliani and Council in preliminary pact on budget.
newsitem.headline: Giuliani and Council in preliminary pact on budget.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani said he has a preliminary pact with the City Council for a $33.4 billion new budget that capitalizes on Wall Street's strong profits by raising spending and cutting taxes.

Giuliani, according to a statement released late Wednesday, also raised his estimate of how big the 1997 fiscal surplus will be by nearly $500 million, projecting the city will have an extra $1.3 billion, largely due to big earnings by Wall Street's banks and brokerages.

But the Republican mayor did not go along with the Council's estimates that the 1998 fiscal year, which starts on July 1, would see as much as $600 million more than his initial estimates, according to the New York Post's Thursday edition. The mayor has the sole power to set revenues, and Giuliani only recognized an extra $364 million.

As a result, Giuliani, who faces an election in November, might be able to raise spending when he modifies the budget in October. As the City Council only votes on the budget as a whole package, and cannot veto specific items, such a strategy gives him more control over the purse strings.

Partly because the city's coffers are full, Giuliani and the Council had an easier time agreeing a new budget, beating the June 10 target date by about six days, than in previous years, when it was a struggle to balance the city's books.
The City Council still must vote on the deal the mayor reached with Speaker Peter Vallone, but that step is considered a formality due to Vallone's strong leadership.

Giuliani said he and the Council agreed to use the 1997 windfall to create an informal $500 million reserve cushion and spend more on education, while cutting overall spending by about $900 million, and moving forward with big tax cuts.

The Council won Giuliani's agreement to spend another $180 million on a range of programs, including funds for cultural institutions like museums and libraries, foster care, youth programs, parks and health clinics, according to the New York Times Thursday edition.

And the Council supported Giuliani's plans to raise spending for education, a flash point during the election year, the Times said. Giuliani had proposed giving another $170 million to the Board of Education, as well as spending almost $1 billion from the city's capital program to pay for computers, school renovation and temporary classrooms.

New York City plans to use the $500 million reserve--which Giuliani called the largest in the city's history--to put $200 million in the general reserve, set aside $200 million to repay fiscal 1999 debt service, and earmark another $100 million for additional debt service that year.
Giuliani said the new pact will reduce out-year gaps by more than he first proposed, although the city still faces a struggle ahead. By 2001, the gap is estimated at almost $3 billion.

The tax cut package adds up to $835 million, but $516 million already has been enacted. The additional $319 million of reductions include a plan to eliminate the city's 4.0 percent sales tax on retail clothing, which would cost $157 million and require Albany's approval.

Giuliani went along with the City Council's proposal to increase the unincorporated business tax credit by $75 million. Other tax reductions included $30 million for the commercial rent tax, and $47 million more for a "proportionate" share of state tax relief, Giuliani said.
And the mayor acceded to the City Council's plan to create a $30 million fund for Emerging Industry Job Development, which seeks to grow sectors like biotechnology and software.

In his budget, Giuliani wanted to cut agencies budgets by $660 million, but the New York Times said the pact likely would reduce give them from $400 million to $500 million less, even as spending is added for other programs.

The mayor also scaled back and delayed an expected settlement with the Port Authority over back rent to $295 million. The revenues from the case, now being arbitrated, were shifted from the fiscal 1998 budget to fiscal years 1999 through 2001.
